title: Explain the Importance of Prohibited Content/Activity and Privacy, Licensing, and Policy Concepts

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Privileged technical access creates duties to preserve evidence, protect regulated information, respect licenses and confidentiality, follow policy, and document actions.
sections.callout: Preserve evidence → protect information → respect licensing → follow policy → document everything.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When evidence, sensitive data, software rights, prohibited activity, or policy requirements appear, choose the authorized legal, procedural, and professional response.

sections.title: Incident Response
paragraphs: Security, privacy, availability, integrity, and policy incidents require established organizational procedures. Do not improvise with potential evidence.

sections.title: Chain of Custody and Escalation

entries.title: Chain of Custody
paragraphs: Records what was collected, who handled it, when possession changed, and where evidence was stored.

entries.title: Informing Management/Law Enforcement as Necessary
paragraphs: Preserve the situation and notify the supervisor, security, legal, management, or law enforcement only as organizational procedure requires.

sections.callout: The technician discovers; authorized leaders decide.

sections.title: Copy of Drive: Data Integrity and Preservation
paragraphs: Create an approved image or copy so the original remains preserved. Avoid actions that alter files, metadata, timestamps, or logs.
sections.callout: Preserve the original; investigate the copy.

sections.title: Incident Documentation
paragraphs: Record what happened, when and by whom it was discovered, affected systems, actions taken, evidence collected, and escalation performed.

sections.title: Order of Volatility
paragraphs: Collect the most temporary evidence first under proper procedures. Memory, running processes, and active connections disappear sooner than persistent storage.
sections.callout: Who handled it → chain of custody; what may disappear first → order of volatility.

sections.title: Licensing, Digital Rights Management (DRM), and End-User License Agreement (EULA)

entries.title: Valid Licenses
paragraphs: Software use must match authorized licensing terms, installation counts, assignments, expiration, and rights.

entries.title: Perpetual License Agreement
paragraphs: Generally permits continued use of a licensed version without recurring subscription payment, subject to the agreement.

entries.title: DRM
paragraphs: Technical controls enforce copying, playback, installation, authorization, or access restrictions.

entries.title: EULA
paragraphs: The agreement defines permitted use, installation count, restrictions, and transfer rights.

sections.callout: Permission → license; terms → EULA; technical restriction → DRM.

sections.title: Personal-Use, Corporate-Use, and Open-Source Licenses
paragraphs: Personal-use rights do not automatically permit business use. Corporate-use licensing authorizes organizational use under its terms. Open-source software still has rules for modification, distribution, attribution, or derivative works.
sections.callout: Open source does not mean ruleless.

sections.title: Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA) and Mutual NDA (MNDA)
paragraphs: An NDA protects confidential information as defined by the agreement. An MNDA protects information exchanged by both parties.

sections.title: Regulated Data

entries.title: Credit Card Payment Information
paragraphs: Limit payment-card access to authorized people and systems.

entries.title: Personal Government-Issued Information
paragraphs: Protect passport, driver-license, and government identifier data.

entries.title: PII
paragraphs: Personally identifiable information identifies or can be linked to an individual.

entries.title: Healthcare Data
paragraphs: Medical information carries strict privacy and security obligations.

sections.callout: Technical ability to open data is not authorization to inspect it.

sections.title: Data Retention Requirements
paragraphs: Law, regulation, contract, or policy may define how long information must remain. Backup provides recovery; retention defines required preservation time.

sections.title: Acceptable Use Policy (AUP) and Prohibited Activity
paragraphs: An AUP defines permitted and prohibited use of company internet, email, devices, software, and data. On encountering prohibited content, do not explore, distribute, or alter it; preserve, report, and document through proper channels.

sections.title: Regulatory and Business Compliance Requirements
paragraphs: Organizations must meet applicable government, industry, contractual, and internal requirements.

entries.title: Splash Screens
paragraphs: An access notice can communicate authorized use, monitoring, security requirements, and AUP expectations before entry.

sections.title: Incident Response Flow
bullets: Recognize the incident or prohibited activity

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Evidence possession history → chain of custody
Preserve storage evidence → drive copy or image
Most temporary evidence first → order of volatility
Source available under terms → open-source license
Payment, government ID, PII, or healthcare information → regulated data

sections.title: Objective 4.6 Exam Trap
bullets: Chain of custody tracks who handled evidence; order of volatility determines what to preserve first.
Preserve the original drive and work from an approved copy.
Personal-use rights do not automatically permit corporate use.
Open-source software still has a license.
License is permission, EULA is the agreement, and DRM is technical enforcement.
NDA is confidentiality; MNDA is mutual confidentiality.
Backup supports recovery; retention specifies how long data must remain.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Identifying or medical data → regulated data
sections.callout: Preserve evidence → protect information → respect licensing → follow policy → document everything.
